result.summary: Pausanias describes sites near the temple of the Cabiri in Boeotia: the plain of Tenerus, the Sphinx's mountain with rival tales of her origin, and Onchestus. He then turns to Thespia, its name, and the story of Cleostratus who killed a dragon with a hooked breastplate.

scenes.title: Plain of Tenerus and Hercules
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes the plain named for the seer Tenerus and a temple of Hercules Hippodetes, who bound the Orchomenians' horses to their chariots.

scenes.title: The Sphinx's mountain
scenes.summary: Different accounts of the Sphinx: a riddling monster, a pirate from Anthedon, or Laius's illegitimate daughter who tested her brothers with Cadmus's oracle. Oedipus learnt the oracle in a dream and defeated her.
scenes.stakes: Claimants to the throne of Thebes risk death if they cannot give the oracle.

scenes.title: Ruins of Onchestus
scenes.summary: About 15 stades on lie the ruins of Onchestus, with a statue of Poseidon and the grove Homer mentions.

scenes.title: Thespia and its name
scenes.summary: Thespia lies under Mount Helicon; its name is derived either from Asopus's daughter or from Thespius of Athens.

scenes.title: Zeus Soter and the dragon
scenes.summary: A dragon demanded a youth each year until Menestratus armed his lover Cleostratus with a hooked breastplate, killing the monster. Pausanias then lists other statues.
scenes.stakes: Cleostratus faces death as the dragon's last victim.

alias_notes.explanation: Means 'horse-binder', from tying the Orchomenians' horses to their chariots.
Saviour, from the rescue of Thespia from the dragon.

notable_quotes.reason: The clever hooked breastplate by which Cleostratus ensured he would kill the dragon.

analysis.text: Pausanias pairs landmarks with competing local traditions, showing how myth explains place names and cult titles.
The rationalised Sphinx as a pirate or royal bastard reflects Greek habit of turning monsters into plausible history.

legacy.text: The Sphinx's riddle and Oedipus's victory became central to Greek tragedy, notably Sophocles' Oedipus Rex.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias cites Homer's mention of the grove of Onchestus, in the Iliad's Catalogue of Ships.

language_notes.text: Hippodetes means "horse-binder" in Greek, which explains the epithet from the story of the tied horses.
"Superior force" means a larger army; this rationalizing version replaces the riddle-monster with a human pirate defeated in war.
"Used subtlety" means she tricked them with a test; "doubtful claimants of the blood royal" means men whose royal birth was uncertain.
Homer mentions the grove of Poseidon at Onchestus in the Iliad's Catalogue of Ships, calling it a "bright grove".
Soter means "Saviour", a common cult title of Zeus.
The hooked plates would catch and wound the dragon as it swallowed him.
Hygiea is the goddess of health; Plutus personifies wealth.

context_notes.text: The Orchomenians were from Orchomenus, a rival Boeotian city, which in myth was defeated by Hercules and made to pay tribute to Thebes.
Laius was king of Thebes and father of Oedipus; Cadmus was the city's founder.
Erechtheus was a legendary king of Athens.
Greek lovers were often an older man and a younger beloved, so Menestratus's devotion fits that custom.

literary_notes.text: The Sphinx is defined by her riddle, which she uses as a weapon against captives.
The dream briefly hints at Oedipus's coming victory over the Sphinx.
The youth goes cheerfully to the monster, and his seeming sacrifice becomes the means of its destruction.
